subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Public Trust and Fear
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Public Trust and Fear.

hook.text: Surveys show that most Americans still don't trust self-driving cars enough to ride in one.

buildup.text: Every robotaxi crash makes headlines, while human-caused crashes that kill 40,000 annually barely do.

discovery.text: People hold robots to a far higher standard than they hold themselves as drivers.

twist.text: Waymo's safety data shows its cars crash far less than human drivers—but one robot crash feels worse.

climax.text: Building public trust may be harder than building the technology itself.

punchline.text: People forgive human error but not machine error.

quiz.question: How do people judge self-driving car safety compared to human drivers?
options: They hold robots to a much higher standard

details.summary: Surveys consistently show that most people are afraid to ride in self-driving cars, creating a trust gap that may be harder to close than the technical challenges of building autonomous vehicles.
details.whyItMatters: Even if autonomous vehicles become statistically safer than human drivers, public fear could prevent widespread adoption. Building trust is as crucial as building the technology itself.
takeaways: Surveys show over 60 percent of Americans fear riding in self-driving cars
A single high-profile crash can set public trust back years
Familiarity through gradual exposure seems to increase acceptance

faq.question: Why do people fear self-driving cars but trust human drivers?
faq.answer: Humans accept risks they feel they can control. Giving up control to a machine triggers loss-of-agency anxiety. People also apply a double standard, tolerating human errors while demanding perfection from machines.

faq.question: What could increase public trust in autonomous vehicles?
faq.answer: Gradual exposure through ride-hailing robotaxis, transparent safety data reporting, millions of uneventful autonomous miles, and positive word-of-mouth from early riders all help build trust incrementally.
